questions.prompt: In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), a set is compact when it is
options: closed, whether or not it is bounded
bounded, whether or not it is closed
questions.explanation: Heine-Borel says that in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the compact sets are exactly the sets that are closed and bounded. An open ball is bounded and not closed, so it is not compact. A line is closed and unbounded, so it is not compact either. Either property by itself is not the theorem.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest radius \(R\) such that the point \((5, 12)\) lies in the closed ball of radius \(R\) about the origin?
questions.explanation: The Euclidean norm is \(\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13\). That is the smallest such radius. The sum of the coordinates is 17, and the larger coordinate is 12. Either of those is larger than the straight-line distance, so neither is the radius of the smallest origin-centered ball.

questions.prompt: The open unit disk is not compact because
options: it does not contain its boundary
questions.explanation: The open unit disk sits inside the closed unit disk, so it is bounded, and it is a nonempty convex set. The unit circle is a set of limit points that the disk does not contain, so the disk is not closed. In the plane, that missing closedness is enough to lose compactness.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to show that the open unit disk is not compact.
questions.explanation: A concrete boundary point comes first, because the failure of closedness is witnessed by that point. It can be approached from inside the disk and it is not a member, so the disk misses a limit point. Only then does Heine-Borel apply: not closed implies not compact. Declaring the disk unbounded would be a different, and false, reason. Invoking compactness before exhibiting the missing limit point skips the property that actually fails.

steps: Name a point on the unit circle.
Note that the point is a limit of points in the disk, and that the point itself is not in the disk.
Conclude that the disk is not closed.
Apply the characterization in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): a set that is not closed is not compact.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest radius of a closed ball about the origin that contains the rectangle \([0, 6] \times [0, 8]\)?
questions.explanation: The farthest corner from the origin is \((6, 8)\), and \(\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\). Every other point of the rectangle is closer. The side lengths 6 and 8 are each too small to cover that corner. The perimeter sum \(2(6+8) = 28\) is not a radius.

questions.prompt: The open unit disk is bounded, and it is not closed. How many of those two Heine-Borel properties does it have?
questions.explanation: Boundedness holds, because the disk sits inside the closed ball of radius 1. Closedness fails, because the unit circle is missing. Exactly one of the two properties holds. Counting both would treat an open disk as closed. Counting neither would deny that a unit disk is bounded.

questions.prompt: Which of these subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are compact?
options: a set of exactly three points
questions.explanation: The closed disk of radius 4 contains its circle and sits inside a ball, so it is closed and bounded. Three points form a finite set: it contains its limit points, and a ball large enough to cover the three points shows it is bounded. The horizontal axis is closed and unbounded. The open disk of radius 4 is bounded and misses its circle, so it is not closed.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest \(M\) such that every one of \((1, 2)\), \((4, -2)\), and \((-5, 0)\) has Euclidean norm at most \(M\)?
questions.explanation: The three norms are \(\sqrt{1+4} = \sqrt{5}\), \(\sqrt{16+4} = \sqrt{20}\), and 5. The largest is 5, from the point \((-5, 0)\). A smaller candidate such as \(\sqrt{20}\) leaves that point out. The sum of the largest coordinates is not the max norm.

questions.prompt: One of these steps is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails.
questions.explanation: The open unit disk is bounded, and the containment in the closed disk of radius 1 is correct. The last step only applies the definition stated above it. That definition is missing closedness. Heine-Borel needs both closed and bounded, and this disk is not closed. The disk is not unbounded, and a positive radius is allowed in the definition of boundedness.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 220" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>disk centered at the origin</title><line x1="28" y1="112" x2="252" y2="112"/><polygon points="252,112 245.6,114.7 245.6,109.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="196" x2="140" y2="28"/><polygon points="140,28 142.7,34.4 137.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="246" y="128" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="32" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><circle cx="140" cy="112" r="64" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.12"/><circle cx="140" cy="112" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A filled disk centered at the origin.
steps: Let U be the open unit disk in the plane.
U sits inside the closed disk of radius 1, so U is bounded.
In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), boundedness alone is the definition of compactness.
Applying that definition to U says that U is compact.
reasons: Compactness in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) also requires the set to be closed, and this disk omits its boundary.
The disk is unbounded, because its radius is a positive number.
Boundedness forbids a finite radius, so the second step already used an illegal ball.

questions.prompt: A continuous real function on a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is guaranteed to attain its minimum when the subset is
options: any closed set, bounded or not
any bounded set, closed or not
questions.explanation: A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum and its maximum. An open interval such as \((0, 1)\) is bounded and the function \(f(x) = x\) has no minimum there. A closed line is closed and unbounded, and a linear function on it is unbounded below. Boundedness without closedness is the open-disk situation. Attainment is the reason compactness shows up in existence arguments.

questions.prompt: On the compact interval \([1, 6]\), the function \(f(x) = (x - 3)^2 + 4\) attains a minimum. What is that minimum value?
questions.explanation: The square is nonnegative and equals 0 at \(x = 3\), which lies in \([1, 6]\). The minimum value is 4. The value at the left endpoint is \((1-3)^2 + 4 = 8\), and the vertex location 3 is the minimizer rather than the minimum value. A continuous function on a nonempty compact set is entitled to attain a value; this one does.

questions.prompt: Which set is closed and unbounded, and therefore not compact?
options: a closed half-space that is not the whole space
questions.explanation: A closed half-space contains its boundary hyperplane, so it is closed, and it runs off to infinity in the inward normal direction, so it is unbounded. It is not compact. The closed unit ball and a two-point set are closed and bounded. The open unit ball is bounded and not closed, which is a different way to fail. An unbounded feasible set is why a stationary-point test still needs a separate existence argument.
